ideas.title: The mosquitoes Colombo released on purpose
ideas.hook: In 2020, Sri Lanka let mosquitoes loose in Colombo on purpose, to fight dengue.
ideas.angle: How Wolbachia bacteria carried by Aedes aegypti block dengue virus inside the mosquito and spread through the wild population without genetic modification.
ideas.why_now: Sri Lanka had a heavy dengue year in 2026 (over 93,000 cases by late August), and the Northeast Monsoon rains of December to early January come just before the quarter.

sources.title: Colombo | World Mosquito Program
Dengue Cases In Sri Lanka Surpass 93,000

research_leads: Look for a peer-reviewed or MoH evaluation of dengue incidence in the CMC-D1 and Nugegoda release areas against control areas; the WMP page reports only preliminary establishment results (data updated June 2023).
Confirm the release dates (pages differ between 2018 and 2020-2021) and the 20 km2 / 240,000 residents coverage.
Get the year-end 2026 NDCU case and death totals.
Check whether the planned Western Province expansion has gone ahead.
cautions: Don't claim the releases reduced dengue in Colombo; no outcome data was found.
Dengue deaths are a sensitive health topic; give symptoms and when to see a doctor only from MoH or WHO guidance.
WMP is the programme's own operator, not an independent evaluator.

ideas.title: The kidney disease with no known cause
ideas.hook: In parts of Sri Lanka's dry zone, farmers' kidneys are failing, and doctors still can't say why.
ideas.angle: How scientists hunt for the cause of a disease (CKDu) that isn't explained by diabetes or high blood pressure: water, metals, agrochemicals, heat, and why no single culprit has been proven.
ideas.why_now: No date hook; it's a long-running local health question. It fits the dry-zone Maha harvest months and pairs with this quarter's water and drought stories.

sources.title: Chronic kidney disease of unknown etiology in Sri Lanka: Quest for understanding and global implications

research_leads: Find recent reviews (2023-2026) of the leading hypotheses (groundwater hardness and fluoride, heavy metals, agrochemicals, heat stress and dehydration).
Get current prevalence figures by district from the Ministry of Health or published surveys.
Note the similar hot spots the RTI brief names in Central America and South Asia.
cautions: The cause is contested. Don't present any single cause (for example glyphosate or arsenic) as settled; use myth_vs_data framing with care.
This is a sensitive health topic for affected communities; avoid fear-based framing and individual patient stories.
The RTI brief dates from 2014, so newer evidence is needed.

ideas.title: Why Sri Lanka needed its own antivenom
ideas.hook: For decades, Sri Lankan snakebite victims were treated with antivenom made from Indian snakes.
ideas.angle: How antivenom is made (venom, horses, antibodies), and why venom differs from region to region, so an antivenom raised against Indian snakes can work poorly on Sri Lankan Russell's vipers and doesn't cover the hump-nosed viper at all.
ideas.why_now: No date hook: snakebite is a year-round rural hazard and paddy work peaks during the Maha season. Check whether the Sri Lanka-specific antivenom has an update before filming.

sources.title: Sri Lanka's antivenom leap forward

research_leads: Find the current status of the AVRI / Instituto Clodomiro Picado / University of Peradeniya polyspecific antivenom (trial results, approval, rollout, local horse facility).
Check the 2016 community survey estimate (over 80,000 bites, 30,000 envenomings, 400 deaths a year) against the published paper.
Look for peer-reviewed evidence on geographic venom variation in Russell's viper (for example PMC8092856, PMC3936006).
cautions: Snakebite first aid must follow current WHO and Sri Lankan medical guidance: no tourniquets, cutting or sucking.
Status information is from 2017; don't imply the new antivenom is in routine use without confirmation.
Draw the snakes as original stylised designs, with no real injury imagery.

ideas.title: Your cinnamon might not be cinnamon
ideas.hook: Most of the 'cinnamon' sold in shops comes from a different tree, and its chemistry is different.
ideas.angle: True Ceylon cinnamon (Cinnamomum verum) and cassia are different plants. Cassia can contain up to about 1% coumarin, while Ceylon cinnamon has only traces, and you can tell the sticks apart by how the bark rolls.
ideas.why_now: It follows the year-end baking season, and cinnamon is one of Sri Lanka's signature crops. The topic isn't tied to a date.

sources.title: Assessment of Coumarin Levels in Ground Cinnamon Available in the Czech Retail Market

research_leads: Confirm the coumarin figures (up to 1% in cassia, about 0.004% in Ceylon) from primary sources, and check the current EFSA tolerable daily intake.
Get Sri Lanka's share of world true-cinnamon production from official export data; trade-press figures conflict (22% vs 80%).
Look into how cinnamon is peeled and quilled (thin layered bark) for the visuals.
cautions: Don't overstate the health risks of cassia, or any health benefits of cinnamon; avoid medical advice.
Sri Lankan trade-press sources are promotional; rely on food-safety agencies.

ideas.title: The ancient lakes that pass water down a chain
ideas.hook: Long before pumps, Sri Lankan farmers built chains of lakes where each one fed the next.
ideas.angle: How the cascaded tank-village system (ellanga gammana) stores monsoon runoff in linked tanks across a micro-catchment, so water used upstream flows on to the next village's tank, buffering both drought and flood.
ideas.why_now: Sri Lanka's 2026 El Niño drought (dried-up tanks, failed crops) and the Maha season brought forward make water storage a live topic this quarter.

sources.title: Sri Lanka designated as a globally important agricultural heritage site
Major El Niño Impact on Sri Lanka in Coming Months

research_leads: Get the FAO GIAHS dossier for the Palugaswewa cascades (the designation year is given as both 2017 and 2018).
Check the 226 plant species figure for the kattakaduwa, bund and tree belt.
Find hydrology studies on how cascades recycle drainage water and recharge groundwater.
cautions: Avoid romanticising: the sources list low farm incomes, youth migration and tank degradation as current threats.
Dating claims for 'ancient' tanks vary; verify before stating an age.

ideas.title: The year Sri Lanka went organic overnight
ideas.hook: In 2021, a whole country banned chemical fertiliser almost overnight. Here's what happened to the rice.
ideas.angle: Why switching a nation's farms to organic inputs in a single season cut yields: what nitrogen does for a rice plant, and why organic sources can't simply replace it at the same speed and scale.
ideas.why_now: The quarter marks five years since the Maha 2021/22 harvest, the first full season under the ban.

sources.title: Sri Lanka's Experiment with Organic Farming Fails Miserably

research_leads: Get official Department of Census and Statistics paddy production for Maha 2020/21 against Maha 2021/22.

Find the peer-reviewed yield estimates: Polonnaruwa farm study (24.5% reduction), the satellite / district working paper (over 30% Maha decline), and the Vavuniya crop-cut comparison; estimates range widely.
Confirm the ban dates (announced April/May 2021, partially lifted November 2021).
cautions: This is politically charged: present data, not blame, and don't attack organic farming in general.
The Breakthrough Institute is an advocacy think tank; use official statistics and peer-reviewed numbers in the script.
Yield-loss figures conflict (roughly 20% to over 50%); give ranges with their sources.

ideas.title: Where did Sri Lanka's blue whales go?
ideas.hook: The biggest animals on Earth used to gather off Mirissa every winter. Lately, almost nobody sees them.
ideas.angle: Sri Lanka has its own blue whale population, with a distinctive 'Sri Lankan' song. The film explains how scientists track whales they can't see (song recordings, fluke photos, transects), and why a 2024 survey suggests sightings fell by more than 90%.
ideas.why_now: December to April is the south-coast blue whale season, with encounters historically peaking in December and April. The Fridtjof Nansen survey results may also be out.

sources.title: Blue whale decline in Sri Lanka tied to climate and human activity
Multiple pygmy blue whale acoustic populations in the Indian Ocean: whale song identifies a possible new population

research_leads: Get the 2024 NARA transect study itself and any 2025-2026 sightings data.
Find the results of the Fridtjof Nansen coastal survey.
Check the Liyanage et al. 2023 seasonal-occurrence paper (J. Mar. Sci. Eng. 11(8):1523), which couldn't be opened here.
Check whether Seychelles photo-ID matches have been confirmed.
cautions: The cause of the decline is speculative (warming, shipping, tourism disturbance, X-Press Pearl); don't assign blame.
A similar disappearance in 2011-2012 reversed, so the drop may be temporary.
729 sightings is not a population count; whales were counted more than once.
Use original drawn whales, not tour footage.

ideas.title: Why elephants and farmers keep colliding
ideas.hook: In 2025, Sri Lanka lost 397 wild elephants, and most of those deaths were linked to conflict with people.
ideas.angle: Why human-elephant conflict happens (shrinking ranges, crops as easy food, fences that move the problem), and what the figures on gunshots, electrocution and train strikes show about where it happens.
ideas.why_now: The full-year 2026 elephant death figures should come out around January, and Cabinet has approved drafting a new national action plan.

sources.title: 397 elephants die in Sri Lanka in 2025, human-elephant conflict a major cause

research_leads: Get final DWC figures for 2025 and 2026 (sources say 2023 was the worst year, at 488).
Find the human death counts for the same years.
Look for peer-reviewed evidence on which measures work (community fences, beehive fences, land-use planning).
cautions: Human deaths make this a sensitive topic; show no gore and no victim stories.
Hakka patas and poisoning are illegal methods; describe them without showing how.
The 397 figure is a mid-December partial count, and some outlets wrongly call it a record.

ideas.title: Flamingos vs power lines in Mannar
ideas.hook: Every winter thousands of pink flamingos land in Mannar, and some never see the wire in front of them.
ideas.angle: Why big, long-necked flocking birds are so bad at dodging cables (wingspan, low manoeuvrability, flying at dawn and dusk), and how wetlands and energy projects can coexist.
ideas.why_now: Greater flamingos winter in Mannar from about November to March, which covers the whole quarter, and three were killed by power lines in 2026.

sources.title: Power lines threaten Sri Lanka's iconic migrant flamingos
Long-legged gregarious pink birds colour the landscape

research_leads: Find evidence on bird-flight diverters and line marking (the IUCN power-line collision report the Mongabay piece cites).
Get the migration timing and flyway route from ornithologists (University of Colombo, Field Ornithology Group).
Check the status of proposed Mannar wind projects near Vankalai Sanctuary.
cautions: Keep it balanced: renewable energy isn't the villain, and placement and mitigation are the point.
Show no dead-bird imagery.
Sources disagree on whether Mannar is the first or last stop on the flyway; check with ornithologists.

ideas.title: The gravity hole south of Sri Lanka
ideas.hook: Just south of Sri Lanka, the sea surface sits more than 100 metres lower than it 'should'.
ideas.angle: Why gravity isn't the same everywhere on Earth: the Indian Ocean Geoid Low, the weakest-gravity patch on the planet, and the IISc model that traces it to hot, light mantle material 300-900 km down.
ideas.why_now: No date hook: it's a surprising local superlative that suits a curiosity slot.

sources.title: Did you know there's a giant 'gravity hole' in Indian Ocean? IISc scientists may have found out why

research_leads: Read Pal & Ghosh (2023) in Geophysical Research Letters for the mechanism and the roughly 20-million-year age.
Check how the geoid is measured (satellite gravity missions such as GRACE and GOCE).
Confirm the 1948 Vening Meinesz discovery and the 3 million km2 extent.
cautions: The mechanism is model-based and debated (plume vs slab remnant); say 'may'.
'Gravity hole' is a nickname: ships and people aren't noticeably lighter there, so avoid exaggeration.
Some coverage contradicts itself about plumes; follow the paper.

ideas.title: The orbit named after a Colombo resident
ideas.hook: The writer who imagined satellites parked in one spot in the sky spent much of his life in Sri Lanka.
ideas.angle: Why an orbit about 35,786 km up takes exactly one day, so a satellite seems to hover over the same spot, and how Arthur C. Clarke's 1945 'Extra-Terrestrial Relays' article popularised the idea of using it for global communications.
ideas.why_now: Clarke moved to Colombo in 1956 and died there on 19 March 2008, so the anniversary of his death falls in the quarter (a non-round year). The story pairs naturally with Raavana-1.

sources.title: The 1945 Proposal by Arthur C. Clarke for Geostationary Satellite Communications
The Surprisingly Interesting Story Behind Why the Geosynchronous Region Around the Earth is Called the Clark Orbit

research_leads: Confirm Clarke's Sri Lanka dates (moved to Colombo 1956; died 19 March 2008) against a primary obituary.
Credit his predecessors (Potočnik / Noordung's book, dated 1928 or 1929 depending on the source) and check the claim about the 1968 Sri Lanka Broadcasting Corporation reminder.
Get the current count of geostationary satellites (the page says over 500 active in 2021).
cautions: Clarke didn't invent the orbit; present him as popularising its use for communications.
Draw an original stylised writer or no likeness at all; don't use photos or film imagery (2001 is copyrighted).

ideas.title: Did a meteorite bring alien algae to Polonnaruwa?
ideas.hook: In 2012, a team claimed a rock that fell in Sri Lanka contained fossils from space.
ideas.angle: How scientists test an extraordinary claim: confirming a rock is a meteorite, ruling out contamination (paddy water full of diatoms), and why the Polonnaruwa diatom claim didn't convince experts.
ideas.why_now: The reported fall was on 29 December 2012, just before the quarter, and January opens the year's meteor-shower season.

sources.title: Claims Of A Meteorite's Ancient Aquatic Fossils Spark Debate

research_leads: Check the Meteoritical Bulletin database for whether any Polonnaruwa fall was ever registered.
Look for later independent analyses of the samples.
Explain what diatoms are and why Earth-like species point to contamination.
cautions: The claim's authors are public researchers; criticise the evidence, not the people.
Avoid 'debunked' unless a formal refutation is found; say 'not accepted'.
Check the timing of any meteor shower before using it as a hook.

ideas.title: One island, two monsoons
ideas.hook: Sri Lanka gets two monsoons from opposite directions, and this year El Niño is meddling with both.
ideas.angle: Why the winds over Sri Lanka reverse twice a year (southwest May-September, northeast December-February), why the central hills make one side wet while the other stays dry, and how El Niño shifts the pattern.
ideas.why_now: The Northeast Monsoon peaks in December-January. Sri Lanka's Department of Meteorology says the 2026 El Niño could be the strongest in nearly 75 years.

sources.title: Major El Niño Impact on Sri Lanka in Coming Months

research_leads: Get the Department of Meteorology's official four-season definition (two monsoons and two inter-monsoons) and the Maha/Yala season months.
Check how the 2026-27 Northeast Monsoon actually turned out (rainfall anomalies, floods).
Find a reliable explainer of the orographic rain-shadow effect of the central highlands.
cautions: Forecasts change; verify what actually happened before narrating it.
Monsoon month boundaries differ between sources; use the Met Department's.

ideas.title: How Cyclone Ditwah turned rain into landslides
ideas.hook: In five days, Cyclone Ditwah dropped so much rain that mountainsides in Sri Lanka slid away.
ideas.angle: Why the damage came mostly from rain rather than wind: saturated slopes on steep central highlands, runoff funnelled into crowded floodplains, and what attribution scientists could and couldn't say about warming's role.
ideas.why_now: The quarter follows the first anniversary (late November), and the Northeast Monsoon brings a fresh landslide-risk season to the hills.

sources.title: Increasing heavy rainfall and extreme flood heights in a warming climate threaten densely populated regions across Sri Lanka and the Malacca Strait
Death toll from Sri Lanka floods, landslides rises to 334: disaster agency

research_leads: Get the final official death toll and rainfall totals from the DMC and the Department of Meteorology (tolls rose quickly in reporting).
Get NBRO guidance on landslide warning signs.
WWA: 1-in-30-year event, 28-160% more intense, with no overall attribution conclusion because the models couldn't match observed trends.
cautions: This is a recent mass-casualty disaster: be respectful, show no victims, and don't make it entertaining.
Don't overclaim climate attribution; the WWA explicitly stopped short of quantifying it.
Include safety messaging only from official agencies.

ideas.title: The trees that slow a tsunami
ideas.hook: Sri Lanka tried planting mangroves after the 2004 tsunami, and only about 3% of the saplings survived.
ideas.angle: How mangroves protect coasts and store carbon, and why Sri Lanka switched from planting saplings to helping mangroves regrow naturally (restoring water flow), work that became a UN World Restoration Flagship.
ideas.why_now: World Wetlands Day falls on 2 February, and the programme is working toward a 10,000-hectare target for 2030.

sources.title: Mangrove Regeneration in Sri Lanka recognized as one of seven UN World Restoration Flagships

research_leads: Find evidence on how much mangroves reduce wave energy (keep claims about stopping tsunamis modest).
Get current figures on restored hectares (about 500 ha since 2015, per the UN page).
Check the claim that Sri Lanka was the first nation to protect all its mangroves in 2015; it is unverified.
cautions: The 2004 tsunami killed over 30,000 people in Sri Lanka; treat it respectfully.
Don't claim mangroves fully stop tsunamis.
The UN page mentions a celebrity announcer; leave that out.

ideas.title: Steel made by the monsoon wind
ideas.hook: More than a thousand years ago, Sri Lankans made steel using nothing but the wind.
ideas.angle: How furnaces built on west-facing ridges at Samanalawewa used steady monsoon winds blowing over their front walls to draw air in and reach smelting temperatures, and how replica tests produced high-carbon steel.
ideas.why_now: No date hook: it pairs with the quarter's monsoon stories and makes a striking local history-of-technology piece.

sources.title: Wind-Powered Furnaces
How Sri Lanka Used Wind to Make Steel

research_leads: Read Juleff, G. (1996) 'An ancient wind-powered iron smelting technology in Sri Lanka', Nature 379, 60-63, for the airflow mechanism and dates.
Reconcile the site counts (41 furnaces at one site; 139 ironworking sites, 77 of them wind-based).
Treat the link to Damascus steel as unverified; check it before mentioning it.
cautions: The Damascus-blade link is speculative; leave it out or flag it clearly.
Explain the aerodynamics accurately (a pressure difference over the wall) rather than 'wind blows into the furnace'.

ideas.title: Sri Lanka's first satellite was the size of a lunchbox
ideas.hook: Sri Lanka's first satellite was a 10 cm cube built in about a year.
ideas.angle: How a CubeSat works (standard 10 cm units, ride-share launch, release from the ISS, photos and a ground station), told through Raavana-1, built by two Arthur C. Clarke Institute engineers at Kyutech for the BIRDS-3 project.
ideas.why_now: No date hook: it pairs with the Clarke orbit story and the growth of small satellites.

sources.title: Four CubeSats successfully deployed from "Kibo"!

research_leads: Confirm the launch (Cygnus NG-11, April 2019), deployment (17 June 2019), mass (about 1.05 kg) and mission end date.
Check whether Sri Lanka has launched or planned follow-up satellites.
Look into the five mission objectives and what the camera actually captured.
cautions: Name the engineers only as public institutional figures, and don't draw them as likenesses.
Don't use Raavana mythology imagery in a way that could offend; keep it to the satellite.

ideas.title: Teaching an AI to speak Sinhala
ideas.hook: Most chatbots are fluent in English and struggle with Sinhala. Here's how researchers in Moratuwa are changing that.
ideas.angle: Why AI models handle 'low-resource' languages poorly (too little text, tokenizers that split Sinhala into fragments), and how SinLlama adds Sinhala tokens and continues training Llama-3-8B on 10 million Sinhala sentences.
ideas.why_now: The SinLlama paper was revised in August 2026, and the model is public; local-language AI is a growing story.

sources.title: SinLlama -- A Large Language Model for Sinhala

research_leads: Read the latest version (v5, 2026-08-31) for results on news categorisation, sentiment and writing-style tasks.
Find a simple, accurate visual of tokenization for Sinhala script.
Check the licence for the Hugging Face release (polyglots/SinLlama_v01) before showing any outputs.
Check whether there are comparable Tamil efforts, for a fair Sri Lankan picture.
cautions: 'Largest Sinhala LLM' is the team's own claim, so don't repeat it.
Show no real chatbot UIs or brand logos; use original drawn interfaces.
The Llama licence covers what can be shown; avoid implying Meta endorsement.

ideas.title: Snakebite is far deadlier than the world counted
ideas.hook: Snakebites may kill up to half a million people a year, and most of them never make the official count.
ideas.angle: How scientists estimate deaths that nobody records: combining hospital records, field surveys and maps to fill gaps where over half of at-risk countries keep no snakebite counts.
ideas.why_now: A new global estimate (274,000 to 513,000 deaths a year) led by researchers from Sri Lanka's University of Kelaniya and LSTM is circulating in the press now; Sri Lanka's dry-zone harvest season keeps snakebite topical.

sources.title: Scientists reveal a hidden snakebite crisis killing up to 513,000 people a year

research_leads: Primary paper: Ediriweera, Kasturiratne et al., 'Estimates of global burden of snakebite: A literature review and geostatistical modelling study', PLOS Medicine 23(8): e1005201, published 2026-08-25, DOI 10.1371/journal.pmed.1005201
Sri Lanka's country-level estimate is in the paper's S4 Appendix; the paper notes regional variation 'even in small countries such as Sri Lanka'
Verify the earlier global estimate the new one replaces (reported as 20,000 to 94,000 deaths) before using a then-vs-now comparison
Check what the WHO and Sri Lanka's Ministry of Health say about first aid and getting to hospital, if the film mentions what to do
cautions: Sensitive health content: no graphic wounds; any first-aid advice must come from official guidance only
Ranges are model estimates with wide uncertainty; present them as ranges, not a single number
The paper itself dates from August 2026; the press coverage is from late October
Draw snakes as original stylised designs; avoid fear-mongering about specific species

ideas.title: Tea and your heart: the hot-cup catch
ideas.hook: Your daily cup of tea might be good for your heart, unless you drink it burning hot.
ideas.angle: What an observational study of nearly 486,000 adults can and can't tell us: tea drinkers had about 11% lower risk of vascular disease, black tea looked more consistent than green, and 'burning hot' tea was linked to higher risk.
ideas.why_now: Published in the Journal of Internal Medicine and covered from 1 November 2026; a natural fit for a country that grows and drinks black tea.

sources.title: Drinking tea may help protect your heart, but there's a surprising catch

research_leads: Paper: 'Habitual tea consumption is associated with lower cardiovascular disease risk', Journal of Internal Medicine (2026), DOI 10.1111/joim.70172; confirm publication date and cohort name
Confirm the 6 to 8 cups per day figure applies only to weekly tea drinkers and what 'moderate strength' means in the study
Source Sri Lankan tea facts (black tea share, consumption habits) separately from official tea-sector data
cautions: Observational association, not proof of cause; say 'linked to', not 'protects'
Cohort was adults in China; don't generalise uncritically to Sri Lankans
No mechanism or temperature threshold was found for the hot-tea risk; don't invent one
Avoid real tea brands or logos

ideas.title: The Nobel-winning trick of switching brain cells with light
ideas.hook: Scientists can flip a single brain cell on and off with a flash of light, and it just won a Nobel Prize.
ideas.angle: How optogenetics works: a light-sensitive channel protein first found in a green alga is put into nerve cells, so light opens the channel and the cell fires.
ideas.why_now: The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine (announced 5 October 2026) went to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for light-gated ion channels and optogenetics.

sources.title: Nobel medicine prize goes to 3 scientists for research into brain activity
Scientists win 2026 Nobel Prize for controlling brain cells with light

research_leads: Check the official citation and press release on nobelprize.org (the site blocked automated fetch)
Confirm the channelrhodopsin and Chlamydomonas alga origin story from the Nobel committee's scientific background
Find a verified example of what optogenetics has revealed (in animals) and any human clinical trials, stated carefully
cautions: Don't draw the real laureates as caricatures; use original characters or text credits
Most work is in lab animals; handle animal research respectfully and don't imply it's a human therapy yet
Avoid 'mind control' framing

ideas.title: Bait traps that teach rice to spot blast fungus
ideas.hook: Rice blast destroys enough rice every year to feed about 60 million people.
ideas.angle: How plants 'see' a fungal attack: immune receptors carry a bait domain that grabs fungal molecules, and scientists engineered receptors that recognise two different fungal signals at once.
ideas.why_now: Science Advances study from the John Innes Centre and Kobe University reported mid-October 2026; rice blast matters to Sri Lanka's paddy farmers in the Maha season.

sources.title: A fungus is threatening the world's food supply. Scientists just found a new defense

research_leads: Paper: 'Engineering plant tandem kinase immune receptors expands effector recognition profiles', Science Advances 12(39), DOI 10.1126/sciadv.aef2426; confirm exact publication date (likely late September 2026)
Verify the '60 million people' figure's original source
Find Sri Lankan Rice Research and Development Institute material on blast disease for the local angle
cautions: Early stage: tested in wheat protoplasts (single cells), not whole plants or fields
Engineered crops are a sensitive policy topic; don't imply farmers can get these plants
Paper date may be earlier than the press coverage

ideas.title: Mixed crops beat drought and floods
ideas.hook: In years of drought and flood, the farms that grew more kinds of crops kept their yields steady.
ideas.angle: Why crop diversification and cover crops make soil act like a sponge: deeper roots leave channels (biopores) that store more water, so yields swing less.
ideas.why_now: Study of 13 Brazilian farms through droughts and floods published 22 October 2026; relevant as a strong El Nino threatens Sri Lanka's rainfall this quarter.

sources.title: Crop diversification protects fields from extreme weather and boosts productivity

research_leads: Paper: Meneghini et al., 'Crop diversification shapes soil multifunctionality under common hydroclimatic extremes', Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment, DOI 10.1016/j.agee.2026.110792
Confirm the 'up to 76% above state average' versus 8% yield figures and what they compare
Look for a Sri Lankan crop rotation or cover-crop example from the Department of Agriculture before claiming local relevance
cautions: Small study (13 farms, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil); don't overgeneralise
Avoid implying a single fix for climate risk to farmers

ideas.title: Trees have 'muscles' that straighten them
ideas.hook: Bend a young tree over and it will pull itself straight again, even without knowing which way is up.
ideas.angle: Trees sense their own shape (proprioception) and grow tension wood on one side that acts like a muscle, then switch sides to stop overshooting.
ideas.why_now: INRAE study in New Phytologist covered 31 October 2026; a playful, visual story that also links to stopping cereal crops from falling over.

sources.title: Scientists discover the hidden “muscles” trees use to straighten themselves

research_leads: Paper: 'Proprioception drives tension wood formation for autotropic straightening and postural control in trees', New Phytologist (2026), DOI 10.1111/nph.71238
Get details of the rotating-platform setup (removes gravity and light cues) for accurate animation
Verify the claimed link to cereal lodging
cautions: Poplar saplings in a lab rig; no quantitative results in the press release
'Muscle' is a metaphor; say so

ideas.title: Sri Lanka's cobra: two million years apart
ideas.hook: Sri Lanka's cobra has been on its own for about two million years. So is it a different species?
ideas.angle: How DNA tells lineages apart: 67 cobras and nine genetic markers show the Sri Lankan spectacled cobra is a distinct lineage, possibly split from India's by changing sea levels, yet scientists stop short of calling it a new species.
ideas.why_now: Study in Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution reported by Mongabay on 13 October 2026, reopening a debate about Sri Lanka's cobra.

sources.title: A study unravels the genetic mystery of a cobra divided by sea

research_leads: Paper: 'Spectacular Saga: Phylogenetics and phylogeography of the Indian spectacled cobra (Naja naja)', Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution vol. 223, 108654 (2026); confirm date
History: 2022 proposal of Naja polyocellata and the 2023 rebuttal by Wuster and Tillack
Verify the land-bridge and sea-level explanation (the article says not proven)
cautions: Taxonomy is contested; do not say it is a new species
Cobras have cultural and religious significance in Sri Lanka; treat respectfully
Avoid encouraging people to handle snakes; draw an original cobra design

ideas.title: A touch that brings bleached coral back
ideas.hook: A bleached coral came back to life in seven weeks, just by touching its healthy twin.
ideas.angle: Why corals bleach (they lose their algae partners) and how touching a genetically identical healthy fragment let algae move across and multiply.
ideas.why_now: Science Advances study from Stanford published 14 October 2026; described as the fastest documented bleaching recovery.

sources.title: A simple touch can bring dying corals back to life in just 7 weeks

research_leads: Paper: 'Rapid coral bleaching recovery via symbiont transfer from healthy corals', Science Advances 12(42), DOI 10.1126/sciadv.aeh1580
Confirm coral species used and lab conditions
For a Sri Lanka tie-in, find a verified source on recent bleaching on Sri Lankan reefs
cautions: Tiny lab experiment (10 fragment pairs); not a reef-scale fix
Avoid implying reefs are 'saved'

ideas.title: Why crocodiles survived the dinosaur asteroid
ideas.hook: The asteroid wiped out the dinosaurs. Crocodiles just went somewhere warm.
ideas.angle: Crocodile relatives followed warm climates for about 250 million years; models show the tropics stayed warm enough after the impact for them to survive.

cautions: Don't make medical claims about cinnamon and blood sugar.
Coumarin safety is a matter of dose. Don't make cassia sound poisonous.
Avoid real brand packaging.

ideas.title: Do goldfish have a 3-second memory?
ideas.hook: Scientists taught goldfish to drive a little robot car on land. Not bad for a 3-second memory.
ideas.angle: Conditioning experiments show fish remember sounds, places and feeding times for months. A 2022 study had goldfish steer a 'fish-operated vehicle' to a target.
ideas.why_now: Evergreen Myth Monday slot; no news peg needed, so it can fill any week of Jan-Mar 2027.

sources.title: Do fish have a three second memory?
Israeli scientists teach goldfish to drive a robotic car on land

research_leads: Identify the Israeli sound-conditioning study cited by Practical Fishkeeping (memory of 4-5 months): the species and the paper.
Read Givon et al. 2022, Behavioural Brain Research, the fish-operated vehicle paper: six goldfish and how the training worked.
Find a peer-reviewed review of fish memory to anchor the 'months' claim.
cautions: The car study shows learning and navigation, not memory span directly. Word it carefully.
Practical Fishkeeping is a hobby magazine, so use primary papers for the numbers.

ideas.title: Are bats blind?
ideas.hook: 'Blind as a bat'? The flying foxes over Sri Lanka find fruit with their eyes.
ideas.angle: All bats can see. Many fruit bats don't echolocate at all and have sharp eyesight, some even seeing ultraviolet, and insect-eating bats use both sight and sonar.
ideas.why_now: Evergreen Myth Monday slot; no news peg needed, so it can fill any week of Jan-Mar 2027. Sri Lanka has about 31 bat species.

sources.title: Are Bats Really Blind?
A newly described cave bat in Sri Lanka indicates presence of more species

research_leads: Confirm the vision and echolocation of the Indian flying fox (Pteropus medius, formerly P. giganteus) from primary literature.
Find the study behind Live Science's claim that bats sometimes prefer sight to sound when hunting.
Check Sri Lanka's species count (31 per Mongabay: 3 fruit bats and 28 insectivorous; other sources say 30).
cautions: Don't link bats to disease scares. Keep the tone pro-conservation.
Footage of real bat colonies may be copyrighted. Draw them.

ideas.title: Do snakes drink milk?
ideas.hook: Snakes don't drink milk. So why do cobras seem to sip from a bowl?
ideas.angle: Snakes are carnivores, and milk isn't part of their diet. A captured cobra that 'drinks milk' has usually been kept without water, and the milk can make it ill.
ideas.why_now: Evergreen Myth Monday slot; no news peg needed, so it can fill any week of Jan-Mar 2027.

sources.title: Debunking Common Myths Surrounding Snakes!

research_leads: Ask a herpetologist or find veterinary literature on whether reptiles can digest lactose. The Wildlife SOS claim of 'lactose intolerant' needs a scientific source.
Find out how widespread the milk-offering belief is in Sri Lanka specifically, compared with India's Nag Panchami.
Find Sri Lankan sources on cobra (naya) welfare and on snake-bite safety for a responsible ending.
cautions: Religious and cultural sensitivity: snakes are revered in Hindu and Buddhist traditions. Explain the biology without mocking anyone's worship.
Wildlife SOS is an advocacy group, and its account of how snakes are captured and starved needs independent support.
Never show handling a venomous snake as something to copy.

ideas.title: How does an elephant drink with its trunk?
ideas.hook: An elephant's trunk isn't a straw. Watch where the water actually goes.
ideas.angle: An elephant sucks water partway up its trunk, widening its nostrils to hold more, then blows it into its mouth. It doesn't drink through the trunk.
ideas.why_now: Evergreen Myth Monday slot; no news peg needed, so it can fill any week of Jan-Mar 2027. Elephants are a local favourite.

sources.title: Engineers surprised by the power of an elephant's trunk

research_leads: Read the original paper (Schulz et al., 2021, Journal of the Royal Society Interface, on Zoo Atlanta's African elephant) for the volumes and flow speeds. SN Explores gives a starting nostril capacity of about 5 L that can grow by more than 60%, and a flow of about 3.7 L per second.
Check whether the findings carry over to Asian, and so Sri Lankan, elephants.
Find a sourced daily water intake for an Asian elephant.
cautions: The study used one African elephant, so don't extrapolate to Sri Lankan elephants without a source.
Draw the elephants rather than using wildlife footage, and avoid scenes of captive elephants used for entertainment.

ideas.title: Is summer when Earth is closest to the Sun?
ideas.hook: On 3 January 2027, Earth will be at its closest to the Sun all year. It's winter for half the planet.
ideas.angle: Earth's orbit is nearly circular. Seasons come from the tilt of Earth's axis, which changes how directly sunlight hits you, not from distance.
ideas.why_now: Perihelion falls inside the quarter: the US Naval Observatory gives 3 January 2027 at 02:33 UT, which is about 08:03 Sri Lanka time.

sources.title: Earth at perihelion – closest to sun – on January 3

research_leads: Confirm the 2027 perihelion time on USNO's 'Earth's Seasons - Equinoxes, Solstices, Perihelion, and Aphelion' service (https://aa.usno.navy.mil/data/Earth_Seasons, no page date). Its data for 2027 lists perihelion on 3 January at 02:33 UT and aphelion on 5 July at 05:06 UT.
Get the perihelion and aphelion distances (about 147 versus 152 million km) and the roughly 3% difference from a NASA or USNO source.
Local twist: near the equator, Sri Lanka's 'seasons' are monsoons rather than summer and winter. Link to the monsoon explainer.
cautions: Never show or suggest looking straight at the Sun.
Give the time in Sri Lanka time (UTC+5:30) and check the conversion.

ideas.title: Can you see the Great Wall of China from space?
ideas.hook: China's first astronaut looked for the Great Wall from orbit. He couldn't see it.
ideas.angle: The wall is very long but narrow. Seeing it from orbit depends on width and contrast, not length, and modern desert roads show up more readily than the ancient wall.
ideas.why_now: Evergreen Myth Monday slot; no news peg needed, so it can fill any week of Jan-Mar 2027.

sources.title: Is China's Great Wall Visible from Space?

research_leads: Read NASA's 2005 feature 'China's Wall Less Great in View from Space' (archived) and the Leroy Chiao zoom-lens photo from the ISS, 2004.
Get the eye-resolution maths: wall width against orbital altitude.
Find which human-made features astronauts do report seeing with the naked eye.
cautions: Show national pride respectfully. Don't mock China.
Don't use real astronauts' likenesses or NASA or CNSA photos without checking licences. Draw them.
'Visible from space' depends on altitude and conditions, so define 'low Earth orbit' and 'naked eye'.

ideas.title: Is there no gravity in space?
ideas.hook: Climb a ladder up to the space station and you'd still weigh about 90% of what you do now.
ideas.angle: Astronauts float because they and their station are falling around Earth together, in free fall, not because gravity has switched off.
ideas.why_now: Evergreen Myth Monday slot; no news peg needed, so it can fill any week of Jan-Mar 2027.

sources.title: What Is Microgravity? (Grades 5-8)

research_leads: Use NASA's figures: the ISS at about 200-250 miles altitude, where gravity is about 90% of its strength at the surface.
Use Newton's cannonball thought experiment for the 'falling around Earth' visual.
Check the ISS orbital speed against a NASA source.
cautions: Don't depict real astronauts or agency logos. Use original characters.

ideas.title: Why your phone's map needs Einstein
ideas.hook: Without Einstein's relativity, your map app would drift by kilometres every day.
ideas.angle: Clocks on GPS satellites run fast by about 38 microseconds a day: general relativity speeds them up and their orbital speed slows them down. Engineers correct for both.
ideas.why_now: Evergreen Myth Monday slot; no news peg needed, so it can fill any week of Jan-Mar 2027.

sources.title: GPS and Relativity

research_leads: Check Pogge's numbers (+45 microseconds a day from general relativity, -7 from special relativity, net +38, and an uncorrected error of about 10 km a day) against Ashby's Living Reviews in Relativity paper.
Explain how a receiver uses timing from 4 or more satellites to fix its position.
Check how the satellite clocks are adjusted before launch.
cautions: Some physicists argue the '10 km per day' figure oversimplifies what receivers actually do. Phrase it as 'errors would build up quickly'.
Don't use the Google Maps or Apple Maps interface. Draw a generic map app.

ideas.title: Lightning never strikes the same place twice?
ideas.hook: The Empire State Building gets hit by lightning about 25 times a year.
ideas.angle: Lightning favours tall, pointed, isolated objects, so the same spot can be hit again and again, sometimes several times in one storm.
ideas.why_now: March is the start of Sri Lanka's first inter-monsoon season (March-April), when afternoon thunderstorms are common. That makes it a timely lightning-safety tie-in.

sources.title: When lightning strikes tall buildings
Video Captures Lightning Striking Empire State Building 3 Times
Meteorological Observations and Instrumental Systems for Meteorological services in Sri Lanka (M.D. Dayananda, Department of Meteorology)

research_leads: The NWS 'Lightning Myths' page (https://www.weather.gov/safety/lightning-myths, no date shown) gives an average of 23 strikes a year, while MPR quoting the NWS gives 25 and Martin Uman gives 20-25. Pick one sourced figure.
Get lightning-death and safety statistics for Sri Lanka from the Department of Meteorology or the Disaster Management Centre.
Explain why tall objects get hit: upward streamers and the shorter distance to the cloud.
cautions: This is safety content: NWS says no place outdoors is safe in a thunderstorm. Use official Sri Lankan advice, and never suggest a risky 'shelter'.
Draw the buildings rather than using real lightning footage.

ideas.title: Do toilets flush the other way south of the equator?
ideas.hook: Tourists pay to watch water swirl 'the other way' at the equator. It's a trick.
ideas.angle: The Coriolis effect is real and steers cyclones, but in a sink or toilet it is far too weak. The shape of the bowl and how the water went in decide the spin.
ideas.why_now: Evergreen Myth Monday slot; no news peg needed, so it can fill any week of Jan-Mar 2027.

sources.title: Does Water Flowing down a Drain Spin Differently Depending on the Hemisphere?
Does water drain in different directions in the Northern and Southern hemispheres?

research_leads: Find the carefully controlled tank experiments that did detect the Coriolis spin (MIT in the 1960s, and the later University of Sydney counterpart in Nature, mentioned by Live Science) and cite them.
Link to cyclones: why the Bay of Bengal cyclones that reach Sri Lanka spin anticlockwise.
Get a rough comparison of the strength of the Coriolis effect against the flow in a household drain.
cautions: Don't say 'the Coriolis effect is a myth'. It is real at large scales.
Don't show real tourist operators or name them.

ideas.title: Why does Sri Lanka have two monsoons?
ideas.hook: Sri Lanka doesn't really have summer and winter. It has two monsoons.
ideas.angle: The winds swing round twice a year. The northeast monsoon (December-February) soaks the north and east; the southwest monsoon (May-September) soaks the southwest and hill country.
ideas.why_now: The northeast monsoon runs December-February, covering most of the quarter.

sources.title: Meteorological Observations and Instrumental Systems for Meteorological services in Sri Lanka (M.D. Dayananda, Department of Meteorology)
Northeast Monsoon Gradually Establishing Over Sri Lanka

research_leads: Get the current season definitions and rainfall maps from the Department of Meteorology (meteo.gov.lk did not load from here).
Explain the mechanism: land and sea heating, and the shift of the ITCZ, from a textbook or IMD source.
Check how the central hills split the rain between the wet zone and the dry zone.
cautions: Keep the film about seasons. Link to any recent flood disaster only carefully, and don't show real victims.
Don't use copyrighted weather-channel graphics. Draw original maps.

ideas.title: Should you drain your phone to 0% before charging?
ideas.hook: Letting your phone die before you charge it doesn't help the battery. It wears it out faster.
ideas.angle: 'Battery memory' came from old nickel-cadmium cells. Lithium-ion cells have no memory and last longest with partial, shallow cycles.
ideas.why_now: Evergreen Myth Monday slot; no news peg needed, so it can fill any week of Jan-Mar 2027.

sources.title: BU-808: How to Prolong Lithium-based Batteries

research_leads: Battery University's BU-808 (published 2010, updated 2026-01-16) says partial discharge is fine, there is no memory, and full discharges should be avoided. It also has a table of cycle life against depth of discharge. Verify the table with a peer-reviewed source.

Apple's 'Batteries - Why Lithium-ion?' page (https://www.apple.com/batteries/why-lithium-ion/, no date shown) says to charge whenever you want, with no need to discharge 100%. Use it as manufacturer support.
Check the nuance that a 'memory-like' effect has been reported in lithium iron phosphate cells (Paul Scherrer Institute).
cautions: Don't name or show phone brands.
Battery safety: avoid any advice about cheap chargers or heat beyond what official sources say.

ideas.title: Does incognito mode make you invisible online?
ideas.hook: Incognito mode hides your browsing from your own phone. It doesn't hide it from the internet.
ideas.angle: Private browsing deletes history and cookies on your device. Websites, your school or employer's network and your internet provider can still see your activity.
ideas.why_now: Evergreen Myth Monday slot; no news peg needed, so it can fill any week of Jan-Mar 2027.

sources.title: Google to destroy browsing data to settle consumer privacy lawsuit

research_leads: Google's Chrome Help page 'Browse in Incognito mode' (https://support.google.com/chrome/answer/95464?hl=en, no date shown) says websites and organisations that manage your network, such as a school, employer or internet provider, may be able to observe activity in Incognito. Quote it.
Check the same point for Safari and Firefox private browsing, to keep the film brand-neutral.
Explain the difference between local and network privacy, and what a VPN does and doesn't do, from a neutral source such as EFF.
cautions: The lawsuit involved a real company, so state it neutrally and accurately. Coverage reports that Google settled without making payments and said the suit was meritless; verify the exact wording before using it.
Don't show real browser interfaces or logos.
Privacy content for teens: don't suggest ways to dodge school or parental controls.

ideas.title: Do microwaves cook food from the inside out?
ideas.hook: If microwaves cooked from the inside out, why is the middle of your leftovers still cold?
ideas.angle: Microwaves mainly heat the outer layers of thick food. The centre warms by ordinary conduction from those hot layers, which is why you stir and let food stand. Microwaved food isn't radioactive.
ideas.why_now: Evergreen Myth Monday slot; no news peg needed, so it can fill any week of Jan-Mar 2027.

sources.title: Microwave Ovens

research_leads: Find a sourced penetration depth for 2.45 GHz microwaves in food. The FDA page states the principle but gives no depth.
Get the FDA's wording that microwave energy doesn't make food radioactive.
Explain how a magnetron and the oven's metal box work, for an animation beat.
cautions: Food-safety content: uneven heating can leave cold spots, so keep the FDA advice to stir and let food stand.
Don't show metal-in-microwave stunts.
Avoid real appliance brands.

ideas.title: The kidney mystery in Sri Lanka's rice bowl
ideas.hook: In some Sri Lankan farming districts, kidneys are failing, and scientists still can't agree why.
ideas.angle: What kidneys do as the body's filters, and how scientists test competing suspects (water, metals, heat, farm chemicals) for chronic kidney disease of unknown cause (CKDu) without a final answer.
ideas.why_now: World Kidney Day falls on Thursday 11 March 2027 (it is held on the second Thursday of March); the 2027 theme is 'Kidneys, Heart, and Metabolism: The Core of Your Health'.

sources.title: World Kidney Day 2027 campaign: Kidneys, Heart, and Metabolism: The Core of Your Health
World Kidney Day: Frequently Asked Questions
Chronic kidney disease of unknown etiology in Sri Lanka (Rajapakse, Shivanthan, Selvarajah; Int J Occup Environ Health 22(3):259-264)

research_leads: Check the 2016 review's prevalence range (15.1-22.9% in Anuradhapura, Polonnaruwa, Badulla) against newer Ministry of Health / NCP data.
Look for the latest consensus papers (2020s) on CKDu causes, including heat stress and genetics.
Confirm what the 2027 WKD campaign materials say, to align the film's tone.
cautions: Contested evidence: no single cause is established; do not blame any one agrochemical, water source or community.
Sensitive health topic for affected families; use drawn characters only, no real patients.
Avoid implying medical advice; point to doctors for symptoms.

ideas.title: The day TB got caught
ideas.hook: For centuries tuberculosis killed without a known culprit, until one microscope slide on 24 March 1882 changed that.
ideas.angle: How Robert Koch identified the bacterium behind TB, and how that discovery made diagnosis and treatment possible.
ideas.why_now: World Tuberculosis Day is 24 March, the date in 1882 when Koch announced the discovery of the TB bacterium.

sources.title: World Tuberculosis Day (WHO)
List of International Days and Weeks (United Nations)

research_leads: Find current WHO Global TB Report figures for the film's numbers.
Check Sri Lanka's National Programme for Tuberculosis Control and Chest Diseases for a local statistic.
Verify how Koch stained and grew the bacterium (Koch's 1882 lecture).
cautions: Health topic with stigma; keep it about the microbe and the science, not about ill people.
Do not give treatment advice; TB treatment must be medically supervised.

ideas.title: How Sri Lanka beat elephantiasis
ideas.hook: A mosquito bite in childhood could mean swollen legs decades later, and Sri Lanka stopped it.
ideas.angle: How lymphatic filariasis (elephantiasis) spreads through mosquitoes and how mosquito control, mass treatment and surveillance let Sri Lanka eliminate it as a public health problem.
ideas.why_now: World Neglected Tropical Diseases Day is 30 January (recognised by WHA decision WHA74(18)).

sources.title: World Neglected Tropical Diseases Day - 30 January (WHO)
Maldives and Sri Lanka eliminate lymphatic filariasis (WHO SEARO news release)

Ask the Anti Filariasis Campaign (Sri Lanka) about post-elimination surveillance.
Check whether WHO has any newer note on Sri Lanka's status.
cautions: Disability imagery can stigmatise; draw symptoms gently or not at all, no real patient photos.

ideas.title: The dhal that makes its own fertiliser
ideas.hook: The parippu on your plate came from a plant that pulls fertiliser out of thin air.
ideas.angle: How pulses (lentils, mung, cowpea) host root bacteria that fix nitrogen from the air into the soil, and why that matters for farms and diets.
ideas.why_now: World Pulses Day (FAO) is 10 February.

sources.title: World Pulses Day | FAO
List of International Days and Weeks (United Nations)

research_leads: Verify the root-nodule / Rhizobium mechanism from a plant science source.
Find Sri Lankan pulse crops grown locally (e.g. mung bean, cowpea) and Department of Agriculture data on production vs imports.
cautions: Keep nutrition claims to what FAO states; avoid diet advice.

ideas.title: Can a forest make its own rain?
ideas.hook: Every tree is a fountain running upside down.
ideas.angle: How trees pull water from the soil and release it as vapour (transpiration), helping clouds and rain over forests like Sri Lanka's Sinharaja.
ideas.why_now: The International Day of Forests (FAO) is 21 March.

sources.title: International Day of Forests | FAO
List of International Days and Weeks (United Nations)

research_leads: Find peer-reviewed sources on transpiration and forest-rainfall feedbacks (e.g. Amazon 'flying rivers') before claiming forests make rain.

cautions: The size of the forest-rain effect is still researched; phrase as 'help make', not 'make'.

ideas.title: Sri Lanka's water staircases
ideas.hook: In Sri Lanka's dry zone, when one village tank fills up, it spills into the next one down the hill.
ideas.angle: How the cascaded tank-village system stores monsoon rain in a chain of small reservoirs to irrigate paddy, buffering floods and droughts.
ideas.why_now: World Water Day is 22 March; the FAO lists the Cascaded Tank-Village System as a Globally Important Agricultural Heritage System since 2017.

sources.title: List of International Days and Weeks (United Nations)
Cascaded Tank-Village System, Sri Lanka | GIAHS | FAO

Check the UN-Water 2027 World Water Day theme when announced.

ideas.title: Wetlands: nature's sponges
ideas.hook: Wetlands are disappearing three times faster than forests.
ideas.angle: How wetlands soak up floodwater, filter it and shelter birds and fish, using a Sri Lankan lagoon or marsh as the drawn setting.
ideas.why_now: World Wetlands Day is 2 February (the Ramsar Convention's day).

sources.title: World Wetlands Day | United Nations

Confirm the Ramsar Convention signing date (2 February 1971).

ideas.title: The underwater meadow the dugong eats
ideas.hook: Underwater meadows can hold up to 18% of the world's ocean carbon, and they feed sea cows.
ideas.angle: What seagrass is (a flowering plant, not seaweed), why its meadows lock away carbon, and who depends on it, such as dugongs in Sri Lankan waters.
ideas.why_now: World Seagrass Day is 1 March (UNGA resolution 76/265).

sources.title: World Seagrass Day | United Nations

Original drawn dugong only; no copyrighted footage.

ideas.title: Why does a tortoise need a passport?
ideas.hook: Some animals can't cross a border without a permit, and a 1973 treaty is why.
ideas.angle: How CITES lists species in appendices and controls their international trade to stop wild populations being emptied.
ideas.why_now: World Wildlife Day is 3 March, the day CITES was signed in 1973.

sources.title: About World Wildlife Day
World Wildlife Day | United Nations

Check the 2027 World Wildlife Day theme once announced and adjust the angle.
cautions: Wildlife trafficking is a crime topic; do not show how to smuggle.
Use original drawn animals.

ideas.title: The rings found by a blinking star
ideas.hook: In 1977 astronomers discovered rings around Uranus without seeing them at all.
ideas.angle: How a stellar occultation works: a star winked out several times before and after Uranus passed in front of it, revealing thin rings.
ideas.why_now: 50th anniversary: on 10 March 1977 observers watched Uranus pass in front of star SAO 158687 and found its rings.

sources.title: Uranus: Exploration - NASA Science

ideas.title: Mars and Jupiter face the Sun head-on
ideas.hook: This February, two planets line up exactly opposite the Sun, one week apart.
ideas.angle: What opposition means (Earth between the Sun and a planet), why the planet looks brightest and rises at sunset, and why Mars only does it every two years or so.
ideas.why_now: Jupiter reaches opposition on 11 February 2027 and Mars on 19 February 2027 (UT); both are easy evening/night targets from Sri Lanka.

sources.title: Celestial Phenomena 2027 (National Astronomical Observatory of Japan)

Verify the ~26-month interval between Mars oppositions.

ideas.title: Two eclipses, two weeks apart
ideas.hook: On 6 February the Sun becomes a ring of fire; two weeks later the Moon barely dims. Same cause.
ideas.angle: Why eclipses come in pairs during 'eclipse seasons', and why a penumbral lunar eclipse is so subtle, with the 21 February pre-dawn view from Sri Lanka.

Lunar Eclipses: 2021-2030 (NASA GSFC)

ideas.title: Uncertainty is not clumsiness
ideas.hook: A century ago, one paper said you can never know exactly where a particle is and how fast it's moving.
ideas.angle: What Heisenberg's uncertainty principle actually says (a limit built into nature, not bad instruments), with a drawn wave-packet analogy.
ideas.why_now: 100th anniversary: Heisenberg's paper 'Über den anschaulichen Inhalt der quantentheoretischen Kinematik und Mechanik' was received by Zeitschrift für Physik on 23 March 1927.

ideas.title: Why the Moon doesn't fall (it does)
ideas.hook: Isaac Newton died 300 years ago this month, and every satellite above Sri Lanka still follows his maths.
ideas.angle: Newton's cannonball idea: the Moon and satellites are always falling toward Earth but moving sideways fast enough to keep missing.
ideas.why_now: 300th anniversary of Newton's death: Westminster Abbey records he died at Kensington on 20 March 1727 (Old Style dating).

sources.title: Sir Isaac Newton | Westminster Abbey
